name: hydranium-root

scripts.check: turbo run build lint typecheck:test test && npm run check:neutral && npm run check:host-load && npm run check:webview-csp && npm run check:exports && npm run check:glob-coverage && npm run check:readmes && npm run check:init-provenance && npm run check:release-trigger && npm run check:exit-trace && npm run check:deps && npm run check:link-tags && npm run check:headers && npm run check:licenses && npm run --if-present check:worklog && npm run --if-present check:public-boundary && npm run check:readme && npm run --if-present check:citations && npm run format:check
scripts.clean: turbo run clean && rimraf packages/*/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo node_modules/.cache/turbo packages/*/node_modules/.vite examples/*/*/node_modules/.vite
scripts.dev:order-flow: cross-env FORCE_COLOR=1 concurrently --kill-others --names "tsc,order-flow" --prefix-colors "blue,magenta" "npm run watch:all" "npm --prefix examples/order-flow/theia-app run watch:all"
scripts.start:order-flow: npm run build:all && npm --prefix examples/order-flow/theia-app start

//check: One clause of the chain is invoked as `npm run --if-present`, and that is a CONVENTION every future clause has to follow or break, not a quirk of this one. A root script whose command reaches into a directory the public-candidate tooling excludes is DROPPED from the candidate's manifest, while `check` itself survives the rewrite because its own command spells script names and no such path — so a plain `npm run <dropped>` leaves the candidate's chain calling a definition its manifest does not have, and exits non-zero on the name. Any clause added over a script outside the public set therefore needs `--if-present` too, and `--if-present` costs nothing where the script IS present: it still runs, and still goes RED on a real violation. Nothing here enforces it and our own gate stays green either way, because the script is present in this tree; what catches a miss is the cold-clone check, which runs this whole chain inside a freshly generated candidate and propagates that run's status rather than swallowing it. Renaming such a script has a second consequence in the other direction: the boundary gate suppresses its own excluded-path rule for exactly the manifest line that declares the script, and it reads that entry back out of THIS file rather than listing it, so a rename reddens the canary guarding that carve-out instead of silently widening the rule. Clause ORDER is by cost, cheapest first, and is worth preserving: the chain is a single `&&`, so a violation caught by a two-second gate should not wait behind a twenty-second one. `check:readme` (a `tsc` per host package over every doc fence), `check:citations` (a `git` call per cited SHA) and `format:check` (prettier over the tree) are the three that cost seconds rather than milliseconds, so they sit at the end; everything else is cheap enough that its position does not matter. The clauses are otherwise independent and may be reordered freely — the one hard constraint is that the turbo clause stays FIRST, because every gate behind it reads built `lib/`.
//clean: The `.vite` entries are the vitest DEP-OPTIMIZER cache, and they are here rather than in a package's own `clean` because no package should have to remember. A package that enables `deps.optimizer` prebundles into `<pkg>/node_modules/.vite/vitest/<hash>/deps_ssr/`, and that directory is the one piece of per-package state nothing else in the repo owns: it is named in no turbo `inputs` (so turbo's hash cannot see it change) and no turbo `outputs` (so turbo never saves, restores or cleans it). When it goes bad — the exposure is two vitest processes over one package, not staleness, since its `_metadata.json` carries a `configHash` and a `lockfileHash` and re-optimizes on a mismatch — every suite in the package fails with `Cannot find module .../deps_ssr/<dep>.js`, which reads as a broken dependency on a package the change never touched. `TURBO_FORCE=true` does NOT help: it re-executes the task, and the task is vitest, which then consults its own cache. Sweeping it here makes `npm run clean` the remedy and keeps it correct for the next package that enables the optimizer. Globs are expanded by the SHELL, as with the tsbuildinfo entry beside them, so a pattern matching nothing reaches rimraf literally and is a no-op.
//langium: langium is pinned to one exact version (4.3.1) to guarantee a SINGLE physical copy across the workspace. @hydranium/langium re-exports langium and the framework packages import langium through it; re-export identity transparency (same AstNode/URI class object via either import path) only holds GIVEN one physical install. Without the pin, single-copy is mere semver-dedup coincidence — a future resolve of @hydranium/*'s ^4.0.0 to a newer minor while another consumer holds an older one would split langium into two installs and break instanceof/nominal identity on AstNode, URI, etc. langium 4.3 is also the first release on the LSP 3.18 stack, and that stack is ONE ATOMIC CHAIN with no independently movable link: langium 4.3.1 → vscode-languageserver ~10.0.1 → vscode-languageserver-protocol ~3.18.1 → vscode-jsonrpc 9.0.1 (exact) + vscode-languageserver-types ~3.18.0. So bump this in lockstep with BOTH the @hydranium/langium dependency AND the vscode-jsonrpc / vscode-languageserver-protocol overrides above. Like those, only takes effect after a from-scratch install.
//overrides: vscode-jsonrpc is pinned to 9.0.1 and vscode-languageserver-protocol to 3.18.2 to collapse the whole LSP wire stack onto ONE physical copy per process. The versions in play disagree: langium 4.3 sits on protocol ~3.18.1 → vscode-jsonrpc 9.0.1 (exact), while @eclipse-glsp/* (2.6.0-2.8.0) still exact-pins vscode-jsonrpc 8.2.0 and Theia still ships protocol 3.17.5 (→ jsonrpc 8). Our backend runs the Langium language server, the GLSP server and the data server in ONE process sharing ONE lsp.Connection, so the copies MUST collapse: ParameterStructures.auto is a singleton compared by identity (===) in connection.js, so a RequestType built by one copy carrying its 'auto' instance, sent over a connection owned by another copy, falls through the switch and throws 'Unknown parameter structure auto' — breaking GLSP server init. We converge UP onto 9.0.1 because the 8→9 move is PACKAGING-ONLY: jsonrpc 9 dropped main/typings for an exports-only map and moved the node transports behind the /node subpath, but its runtime API is unchanged — which is why GLSP's own chore/vscode-jsonrpc-9 branch needed ZERO source changes and GLSP's compiled 8.2-era JS runs against 9.0.1 unmodified. That packaging regression is repaired locally by patches/vscode-jsonrpc+9.0.1.patch (patch-package, wired to postinstall): it re-adds main/typings plus the root node.js/browser.js re-export shims and adds the 'default' export condition 9.x omits on the /node and /browser subpaths, so consumers on classic moduleResolution: Node (the theia-client packages, Theia itself) keep resolving. Pinning the protocol at 3.18.2 holds the other end of the chain (3.18.2 → jsonrpc 9.0.1 exact + types 3.18.0) so a protocol-3.17.5 consumer cannot drag a second jsonrpc 8 copy back in. Overrides AND patches only take effect after a from-scratch install (rm -rf node_modules + package-lock.json); a lockfile-only delete leaves stale nested copies.
//patches: TWO patches, and they are different KINDS. `vscode-jsonrpc+9.0.1.patch` repairs a packaging regression we depend on and is described under `//overrides`; it stays until 9.x republishes the entry points. `vitest+4.1.11.patch` is SCAFFOLDING for one open investigation and carries an explicit removal trigger. What it buys: vitest 4's `emitUnexpectedExit` is declared with NO parameters, so the `(code, signal)` Node's `exit` event hands it is discarded and a dead worker reports only `Worker exited unexpectedly`. The patch gives the handler `(exitCode, signal)` and prints both plus the hex, masking with `>>> 0` because Windows may hand back the status signed. It was built to read that code as an NTSTATUS, on the reasoning that it is the one fact telling an access violation (0xC0000005) apart from a V8 CHECK (0xC0000409) and from a shutdown race (0xC000013A). It has since ANSWERED that question by ruling out the whole family: three separate captures on `windows-2025` — `@hydranium/cli`, `@hydranium/glsp-client-theia` and the order-flow server, the last two having lost no test file at all — every one of them reads `code=1 hex=0x00000001 signal=null`. So the worker made an ORDINARY non-zero exit whose output nobody saw, which is the same shape as the silent `tsc`, `eslint` and `npm` deaths in the captured task logs, and is what `scripts/trace-exits.cjs` exists to attribute (see `//trace-exits`). The patch stays because it is what tells a worker death apart from a tool's, and because its message is the only place the worker's code appears at all. The `[hydranium-patch]` marker in the message is deliberate: it is how a reader of an uploaded `gate.log` tells a patched run from one where the patch silently did not apply. REMOVE IT when either the crash is diagnosed or vitest moves off 4.1.11, whichever comes first — the fix that surfaces the code upstream (vitest PRs #10587 and #10964) landed in 5.0.0 only and was never backported, 4.1.11 being the last v4, so a version bump makes the patch redundant rather than merely stale. The bump reports itself: the target is a CONTENT-HASHED chunk filename (`dist/chunks/cli-api.<hash>.js`), so a new vitest has no such file and `patch-package` fails to apply — non-zero on CI, where it defaults to error-on-fail, and a warning locally. Re-derive with `npx patch-package vitest` rather than hand-editing the diff, and note that it shells out to whatever `npm` is FIRST ON PATH to install a pristine copy: an npm older than this repo's `packageManager` pin dies in arborist with `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'edgesOut')`, which patch-package reports as a bare spawn-status object naming nothing. Adding or removing a patch also retires the CI `node_modules` cache, which hashes `patches/**` into its key — necessary, because a cache HIT skips `npm ci` and therefore `postinstall`, so a restored tree carries whichever patches were current when it was saved.
//postinstall: Two things, and the second one MUST NOT be allowed to fail. `patch-package` applies the patches described under `//patches`. `scripts/postinstall-hint.mjs` names the cold-clone false green: `hydranium-cli`'s `lib/` is generated and gitignored, so on a fresh clone npm silently skips linking its bin and the failure then surfaces in an EXAMPLE as `hydranium-cli: not found` (exit 127), naming neither the cause nor this package. The hint WARNS and never exits non-zero, because on a genuine first install that `lib/` is legitimately absent — that is the state the documented sequence starts from, so failing here would break the very sequence the hint recommends, which is the original bug one layer up. It lives in `postinstall` rather than in a workspace `prepare` because a `prepare` runs BEFORE the root patch is applied and two attempts at that shape died on install ordering; running after the install means it knows the answer instead of racing it. A registry consumer runs the published package's own scripts and never this root's, so nothing here reaches one.
//trace-exits: `scripts/trace-exits.cjs` is SCAFFOLDING for the same investigation as the vitest patch above, and carries the same kind of removal trigger: delete it, `check:exit-trace`, its self-test and the wiring in `ci.yml`'s gate step once the Windows silent-exit failure is diagnosed. What it buys: a `--require` preload that records why a Node process exited non-zero, into one file per process under the directory `HYDRANIUM_EXIT_TRACE_DIR` names. It sits under EVERY Node process rather than on any one tool because the victim is not a tool — captured `.turbo/*.log` files show the identical silent non-zero exit from `tsc --noEmit` with no diagnostic printed, from `eslint` (which exits 1 only when it found something it would have printed), from a vitest fork worker, and from an intermediate `npm run` that never printed npm's own `Lifecycle script … failed` block. It records to FILES because both streams a dying process would otherwise use are already known to lose exactly this: vitest pipes a fork's stdout and stderr into its own console interception, which attributes output to the running test and drops what arrives after one finishes, and turbo merges sixty-six tasks' streams into one pipe. Reading a record: an `uncaught` field names the exception and closes the case; an `exitCall` stack with no `uncaught` names the library line calling `process.exit` and closes it; NEITHER, with a non-zero `code`, means the tool chose that code deliberately, which for eslint would mean real findings whose output was lost; and NO RECORD AT ALL for a task turbo reported as failing means the process never reached a JS exit handler, which moves the question to external termination. That last outcome is why `check:exit-trace` is in the chain rather than optional — a recorder that has silently stopped installing leaves the same empty directory as the finding — and why the gate step proves the recorder live before running anything. Three constraints it must keep, each asserted by the self-test: never write to stdout or stderr (subcommand tests assert on a spawned process's exact stdout), never change an exit code (which is why it hooks `uncaughtExceptionMonitor` and not `uncaughtException`, the latter SUPPRESSING the crash it is meant to observe), and leave no file behind for a process that exits 0. One known blind spot: `@hydranium/conformance`'s jest tier sets `NODE_OPTIONS` through `cross-env`, REPLACING the inherited value, so the preload does not reach that process.
//vite: vite is a DIRECT devDependency pinned to ~8.0.16 even though nothing imports it: we consume it as vitest's transform pipeline, and vite 8.1.x — which switched to rolldown 1.1.x — mis-transforms LEGACY TypeScript decorators. Every test file declaring an `@injectable()` class then fails to load with an opaque `SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token` before a single import runs (the inversify-based state/harness tests). vite 8.0.16 + rolldown 1.0.3 transform the same files correctly. It is declared as a devDependency rather than in `overrides` because there is no version CONFLICT to resolve: nothing else in the workspace declares a vite range, vitest simply asks for `^6 || ^7 || ^8`, and a fresh resolve takes the newest 8.x. A direct dependency states what we actually consume, stays visible to `npm ls` / audits, and leaves `overrides` for the single-physical-copy identity problems above. The trade-off is that it DEDUPES rather than forces, so after a from-scratch install re-verify that exactly ONE vite is installed and it is 8.0.x. The pin is transform-only — no product code depends on vite. Drop it once vite/rolldown fix the decorator transform; verify with `npm --prefix packages/glsp-server run test`.
